usage: 알 is the natural counter for round fruit like peaches.
A common allergy in Korea; worth knowing this exact phrase.
물복숭아(juicy/soft) and 딱딱한 복숭아(firm); locals debate which is better.
무르다 → 물렀다; peaches bruise and spoil fast.
examples: 여름 되면 복숭아가 진짜 맛있어요.
When summer comes, peaches are really delicious.
복숭아 is a signature summer fruit here.
저는 단단한 복숭아보다 물복이 좋아요.
I prefer soft peaches over firm ones.
물복 is the casual short form for the juicy type.
복숭아는 금방 무르니까 빨리 먹어요.
Peaches go soft quickly, so eat them fast.
무르다 describes fruit getting overripe and mushy.
nuance: 복숭아 is one of Korea's most beloved summer fruits, and people genuinely split into two camps: 물복 (soft, juicy) versus 딱복 (firm, crunchy). It's also one of the more common food allergies here, so being able to say 복숭아 알레르기 있어요 can actually matter at a restaurant or a friend's house.
mistakes: Counting 복숭아 with 개 sounds off for fruit — 한 알 or 한 개 are both heard, but 알 is more natural at a market.
Saying 복숭아가 썩었어요 (rotten) when you just mean it's soft/overripe — that's 물렀어요.

usage: One bag of Korean melons, please
Often sold by the 봉지 (bag) at markets and marts.
We peel and eat Korean melon
깎다 = to peel; the yellow skin is removed first.
성주 is the region famous for the best 참외.
The yellow ones are the tasty ones
Ripe 참외 turns bright yellow with white stripes.
examples: 참외는 한국에만 있는 과일이라 외국인들이 신기해해요.
Chamoe is a fruit found mainly in Korea, so foreigners find it novel.
참외 rarely appears abroad, so it surprises newcomers.
여름에 참외 깎아서 냉장고에 넣어 두면 시원해요.
In summer, peel chamoe and keep it in the fridge for a cool treat.
Chilled 참외 is a classic summer snack.
이 참외 진짜 달다, 한번 먹어 봐.
This chamoe is really sweet, try a piece.
달다 = sweet; ripe 참외 is honey-sweet.
nuance: 참외 is the bright-yellow Korean melon that's almost unknown outside Korea, so it's a fun, very local fruit to learn. It's a summer staple eaten peeled and chilled, and the variety from 성주 is treated as the gold standard the way certain regions are famous for specific produce.
mistakes: Translating 참외 as just 'melon' — that's 멜론, a different fruit; 참외 is its own thing.
Eating 참외 with the peel on; Koreans peel off the yellow skin first (깎아 먹다).

usage: Counted with 알 like other small round fruit.
새콤하다 = pleasantly sour; plums are tangy.
제철 = peak season, roughly early-mid summer.
씨 = seed/pit; there's a hard stone in the center.
examples: 자두는 새콤달콤해서 여름에 자주 먹어요.
Plums are sweet-and-sour, so I eat them often in summer.
새콤달콤 captures the tart-sweet plum flavor.
자두 씻어서 그냥 통째로 먹으면 돼요.
Just wash the plums and eat them whole.
통째로 = whole; you bite around the pit.
마트에 자두 나온 거 보니까 여름이네요.
Seeing plums at the mart, I can tell it's summer.
Seasonal fruit appearing signals the season.
nuance: 자두 (plum) is a small, tart-sweet summer fruit you'll see piled up at markets from around June. Its flavor is described as 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour), and unlike 복숭아 you usually eat it whole and unpeeled, just biting around the central 씨 (pit).
mistakes: Confusing 자두 (plum) with 자몽 (grapefruit) — similar-sounding but completely different fruit.
Trying to peel 자두 like a peach; the thin skin is eaten as-is.

usage: Firm sweet persimmon vs. soft ripe persimmon
단감 is crunchy; 홍시 is soft and jelly-like.
떫다 = astringent/puckery; unripe 감 is mouth-drying.
곶감 is a chewy dried sweet, popular in winter.
Counted with 개; an autumn fruit.
examples: 가을에는 감이 제철이라 엄청 달아요.
In autumn persimmons are in season, so they're super sweet.
감 is an iconic fall fruit.
저는 딱딱한 단감을 더 좋아해요.
I prefer the firm, crunchy persimmon.
단감 is the crisp variety eaten like an apple.
덜 익은 감은 떫어서 못 먹어요.
Unripe persimmons are too astringent to eat.
떫다 is the puckery taste of underripe 감.
nuance: 감 (persimmon) is a quintessential autumn fruit in Korea, sold as the crunchy 단감 or the soft, spoon-eaten 홍시, and dried into chewy 곶감 for winter. The key flavor word is 떫다 (astringent) — an unripe persimmon dries out your mouth, a sensation 20-30s here describe constantly.
mistakes: Using 감 by itself when you mean a specific type — at a market, specify 단감 (firm) or 홍시 (soft).
Saying 감이 써요 (bitter) for an unripe one; the right word is 떫어요 (astringent).

usage: 망고 빙수 is a hugely popular summer café dessert.
익다 = to ripen; ripe mango is soft and fragrant.
냉동 = frozen; sold in bags for smoothies and snacks.
A common café and convenience-store drink flavor.
examples: 여름에 카페에서 망고 빙수 꼭 먹어요.
In summer I always get mango bingsu at a café.
망고 빙수 is a seasonal café must-have.
망고는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 사 먹어요.
Mango is a bit pricey, but I buy it once in a while.
Imported 망고 reads as a small treat.
냉동 망고로 스무디 만들어 먹어요.
I make smoothies with frozen mango.
냉동 망고 is a cheap, convenient option.
nuance: 망고 (mango) is an imported fruit that feels a little special and pricey in Korea, so it shows up most as a treat — above all the wildly popular 망고 빙수 (mango shaved ice) that defines summer café menus. Frozen 냉동 망고 is the budget-friendly way people enjoy it at home in smoothies.
mistakes: Assuming 망고 is cheap year-round like apples — fresh mango is often a pricier, occasional buy.
Saying 애플망고 and 망고 interchangeably — 애플망고 is the small, sweeter premium type sold separately.

usage: Sold in small 팩 (packs/punnets), not loose.
냉동 = frozen; a cheaper, year-round option.
Blueberries are good for your eyes
A widely repeated health belief in Korea.
A common flavor for yogurt and smoothies.
examples: 아침에 요거트에 블루베리 넣어 먹어요.
In the morning I add blueberries to my yogurt.
A typical healthy-breakfast habit.
블루베리는 눈 건강에 좋다고 해서 자주 사요.
They say blueberries are good for eye health, so I buy them often.
Reflects the common 눈에 좋다 belief.
생블루베리가 비싸서 냉동으로 사요.
Fresh blueberries are expensive, so I buy frozen.
냉동 블루베리 is the practical choice.
nuance: 블루베리 (blueberry) is marketed in Korea as a health food — you'll constantly hear 블루베리가 눈에 좋아요 (good for your eyes) — and it's a staple of yogurt bowls and smoothies among health-conscious 20-30s. Fresh ones come in small pricey 팩, so many people default to cheaper 냉동 (frozen) bags.
mistakes: Counting 블루베리 with 개 for the whole container — buy it as 한 팩 (one pack).
Spelling it 블루베리 vs. 블루배리 — the correct loanword is 블루베리.

usage: 골드키위 is sweeter; 그린키위 is tarter.
Counted with 개; a small fuzzy fruit.
깎다 = to peel off the fuzzy brown skin.
시큼하다 = sour; unripe green kiwi is quite tart.
examples: 골드키위가 그린키위보다 더 달아요.
Gold kiwi is sweeter than green kiwi.
골드키위 is the sweeter, premium type.
키위는 반으로 잘라서 숟가락으로 떠먹어요.
I cut the kiwi in half and scoop it with a spoon.
떠먹다 = to scoop and eat; a common way to eat kiwi.
덜 익은 키위는 좀 시큼해요.
An underripe kiwi is a bit sour.
시큼하다 describes the tartness of unripe kiwi.
nuance: 키위 (kiwi) is a popular everyday fruit in Korea, split into the sweeter 골드키위 and the tarter 그린키위 you'll see labeled separately at the mart. Beyond peeling it, a very common local habit is to halve it and 떠먹다 (scoop it out with a spoon), and unripe ones are described as 시큼하다 (sour).
mistakes: Eating the fuzzy brown skin — Koreans always peel 키위 or scoop it out with a spoon.
Assuming all 키위 taste the same; 골드키위 (sweet) and 그린키위 (tart) are noticeably different.

usage: 데치다 = to blanch briefly in boiling water.
송이 is the counter for a head/cluster.
살짝 = lightly; keeps it green and crunchy.
초고추장 is the standard dip for blanched veg.
examples: 브로콜리는 살짝 데쳐서 초고추장에 찍어 먹어요.
Blanch the broccoli lightly and dip it in chili-vinegar sauce.
데치다 + 초고추장 is the classic Korean way to eat it.
다이어트할 때 브로콜리 많이 먹어요.
When I'm dieting, I eat a lot of broccoli.
브로콜리 is a go-to healthy/diet vegetable.
브로콜리를 너무 오래 삶으면 물러져요.
If you boil broccoli too long, it gets mushy.
물러지다 = to turn soft/mushy from overcooking.
nuance: 브로콜리 (broccoli) is firmly part of healthy and diet eating in Korea, often appearing on 닭가슴살 (chicken breast) diet plates. The very Korean way to serve it is lightly 데친 (blanched) and dipped in 초고추장 (sweet chili-vinegar paste), and locals warn that overboiling makes it 물러지다 (mushy).
mistakes: Counting 브로콜리 with 개 — a whole head is 한 송이.
Serving 브로콜리 raw and plain; the expected style is blanched with 초고추장.

usage: Sold in red, yellow, orange, and green colors.
Counted with 개; firm and glossy.
Sliced bell pepper in a salad
썰다 = to slice; common raw in salads.
Unlike 고추, 파프리카 is sweet, not hot.
examples: 파프리카는 색깔별로 맛이 조금씩 달라요.
Bell peppers taste slightly different by color.
Red ones are sweeter than green ones.
저는 파프리카 생으로 썰어서 그냥 먹어요.
I just slice bell peppers and eat them raw.
생으로 = raw; 파프리카 is crunchy and sweet.
볶음 요리에 파프리카 넣으면 색이 예뻐요.
Adding bell pepper to a stir-fry makes it colorful.
Often added for color and crunch.
nuance: 파프리카 is the sweet bell pepper (from Dutch 'paprika'), totally distinct from the spicy 고추 — a distinction newcomers must learn. It's a colorful, crunchy vegetable Koreans eat raw in salads or sliced as a snack, and it's a major Korean export, so it's everywhere and quite affordable.
mistakes: Confusing 파프리카 (sweet bell pepper) with 고추 (hot chili) — 파프리카 is not spicy at all.
Calling it 피망 in every case; 피망 is the smaller, slightly bitter green pepper, sold separately.

usage: 볶음 = stir-fry; a common 반찬 (side dish).
나물 = seasoned vegetable side; soft and savory.
Counted with 개; long and purple in Korea.
물컹하다 = soft and squishy; its cooked texture.
examples: 가지나물은 호불호가 좀 갈려요.
Seasoned eggplant is a love-it-or-hate-it dish.
호불호가 갈리다 = opinions are divided on it.
가지를 기름에 볶으면 부드러워져요.
When you stir-fry eggplant in oil, it gets soft.
Eggplant soaks up oil and softens.
저는 어릴 때 가지를 싫어했는데 지금은 좋아해요.
I disliked eggplant as a kid but like it now.
A common shift in taste for 가지.
nuance: 가지 (eggplant) in Korea is the long, slender purple type, eaten mainly as the side dishes 가지나물 (seasoned steamed) and 가지볶음 (stir-fried). Its soft, 물컹한 texture makes it a classic 호불호 (love-it-or-hate-it) vegetable, especially among kids, so it comes up a lot in conversations about food preferences.
mistakes: Note 가지 is also a counter/word for 'kind, type' (한 가지) — context tells you it's the vegetable.
Expecting a round Western eggplant; Korean 가지 is long and thin.

usage: 군- = roasted; a beloved winter street snack.
Give me one sweet potato, please
Slang: 고구마 = a frustrating, stifling situation.
꿀- = honey; a sweeter, moister variety.
examples: 겨울엔 길거리에서 군고구마 사 먹는 게 최고예요.
In winter, buying roasted sweet potato on the street is the best.
군고구마 is an iconic winter snack.
고구마는 다이어트할 때 밥 대신 먹기도 해요.
People sometimes eat sweet potato instead of rice when dieting.
고구마 is a popular carb swap.
그 드라마 진짜 고구마 같아서 답답했어.
That drama was so 'sweet potato' — really frustrating.
고구마 = a stifling, no-payoff plot or situation.
nuance: 고구마 (sweet potato) is both a beloved food — especially winter 군고구마 (roasted) and the diet-friendly carb swap for rice — and a piece of modern slang. Calling something 고구마 means it's frustrating and stifling (like eating dry sweet potato with no water), the opposite of the satisfying 사이다, so 20-30s use it constantly about dramas and annoying situations.
mistakes: Confusing 고구마 (sweet potato) with 감자 (regular potato) — different foods and different slang.
Missing the slang: 고구마 같다 isn't about food, it means 'frustrating/stifling.'

usage: 찌다 → 찐; a popular summer street snack.
Counted with 개 for a cob.
통조림 = canned; used in salads and on pizza.
A common roasted-corn tea, drunk hot or cold.
examples: 여름에 길에서 찐 옥수수 사 먹어요.
In summer I buy steamed corn from street stalls.
찐 옥수수 is a classic warm-season snack.
샐러드에 옥수수 통조림 넣으면 맛있어요.
Adding canned corn to a salad makes it tasty.
옥수수 통조림 is a convenient pantry staple.
식당에서 물 대신 옥수수차 주는 데 많아요.
Many restaurants give corn tea instead of water.
옥수수차 (or 보리차) is a common free table drink.
nuance: 옥수수 (corn) shows up in everyday Korean life in three big ways: 찐 옥수수 (steamed on the cob) as a summer street snack, canned 옥수수 통조림 sprinkled on salads and even pizza, and 옥수수차 (corn tea) served free at many restaurants. Recognizing all three covers where you'll actually meet the word.
mistakes: Counting 옥수수 with 송이 — a cob is 한 개, not 한 송이.
Forgetting 옥수수차 is a tea, not a corn drink with kernels; it's a roasted-grain brew like 보리차.
